excerpt: A lift going below the ground floor is where most kids first meet a negative number. Here is a clear, practice-first guide to integers for Grade 6 — the number line, ordering, absolute value, and the add-and-subtract rules that trip everyone up — with a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Press ‘B2’ in a mall lift and you have just used a negative number without thinking about it. That is where I start with integers grade 6 negative numbers — not with a rule to memorise, but with the lift, the thermometer showing −2°C in Shimla, and the cricket score where a batsman is ‘3 runs in the red’ against the target. Integers are simply the counting numbers, their negatives, and zero, all lined up in order. The trouble is never the idea. It is the moment a child has to compute −5 − 6 and their hand hovers over the page.

This is a skill-practice guide. We will fix four things in order: reading the number line, comparing and ordering, absolute value, and the rules for adding and subtracting. Get these solid and the rest of Class 6 arithmetic stops feeling like a trap.

The integer number line is the whole game

Draw a line, mark 0 in the middle, positives to the right, negatives to the left. Every question about integers grade 6 negative numbers can be answered by pointing at this line. Two facts do most of the work:

  • The further right you go, the bigger the number. So 3 > 1, and also −1 > −3.
  • Numbers the same distance from 0 on opposite sides are called opposites: 4 and −4, 9 and −9. Their sum is always 0.

That first fact is where most mistakes live. A child who is sure that 7 is bigger than 3 will confidently say −7 is bigger than −3 — because 7 ‘feels’ bigger. On the line, −7 sits far to the left of −3, so it is actually smaller. I make students physically point left before every negative comparison. It looks slow. It saves them a whole term of errors.

Comparing and ordering

To compare, put both numbers on the line and read left to right. To order a list, the same rule scales up. Try arranging −8, −3, 0, 2 from least to greatest: the most-negative number is smallest, so it goes first — −8, −3, 0, 2.

A reliable check for parents: temperature. Ask ‘which is colder, −8°C or −3°C?’ Colder is more negative is further left is smaller. −8 wins. Kids who freeze on abstract symbols usually answer the weather version instantly, and you can carry that intuition straight back to the number line.

Absolute value: distance, never direction

The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0, so it is never negative. We write it with two straight bars: |−15| = 15 and |15| = 15. Distance does not care which way you walked. This is the one place where the negative sign genuinely disappears — a useful anchor when the sign rules start piling up.

Absolute value matters because the addition and subtraction rules below are stated in terms of it. If a child cannot quickly say that |−6| is 6, the rules will feel like magic words rather than steps.

The rules for adding integers

Here is the part everyone wants. There are only two cases, and they both use absolute value.

SituationWhat to doExample
Same signs (both + or both −)Add the absolute values, keep the common sign−6 + (−4) = −10
Different signsSubtract the smaller absolute value from the larger, take the sign of the larger−9 + 5 = −4
OppositesThey cancel to zero7 + (−7) = 0

Think of it as money. Same signs are two debts stacking (−6 and −4 owed is −10 owed) or two credits stacking. Different signs are a debt meeting a credit — whoever is bigger wins, and the answer wears their sign. For −9 + 5, the debt of 9 beats the credit of 5, so you are still 4 in the red: −4.

Subtracting integers: add the opposite

Subtraction looks scarier than it is because there is one trick that turns every subtraction into an addition you already know: keep, change, change. Keep the first number, change the minus to a plus, change the sign of the second number.

So 8 − (−3) becomes 8 + 3 = 11. Subtracting a negative adds — taking away a debt makes you richer. And −5 − 6 becomes −5 + (−6) = −11, which is now just the same-sign rule from the table above.

The one that catches everyone

‘Subtracting a negative is the same as adding’ is the single most counter-intuitive fact in the whole topic. Do not rush past it. I get students to say the double-negative sentence out loud — ‘take away a take-away’ — and pair it with the debt story until it stops feeling like a rule pulled from thin air. Rush this and every mixed-practice sheet turns into a guessing game.

How to practise so it sticks

Twenty minutes of the right practice beats an hour of copying answers. My honest recommendation: do not mix subtraction in until adding is genuinely automatic. A common mistake is to hand a child a page of everything at once; they end up applying the addition rule to a subtraction question and lose confidence. Build in layers — a day of same-sign addition, a day of different-sign, then convert subtractions with keep-change-change, and only then mix it all up so the child has to decide which rule fits.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The eight-question quiz below covers exactly what we walked through — ordering, absolute value, and both sign rules for integers grade 6 negative numbers. Read each explanation, especially for anything missed. When your child is ready for longer graded practice with a full answer key, the printable worksheet at the end has plenty of it.

quiz.title: Grade 6 Integers & Negative Numbers Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on the number line, ordering, absolute value and the add-and-subtract rules. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 6 integers: ordering, absolute value, adding and subtracting

questions.explanation: Same signs: add the absolute values 6 + 4 = 10 and keep the common negative sign, giving −10.
Different signs: subtract 5 from 9 to get 4, then take the sign of the larger absolute value (9 is negative), giving −4.
Keep, change, change: 8 − (−3) becomes 8 + 3 = 11. Subtracting a negative adds.
On the number line −7 sits to the right of −12, so −7 is the greater number.

questions.q: What is the absolute value of −15, written |−15|?
questions.explanation: Absolute value is distance from 0 and is never negative, so |−15| = 15.

questions.q: Order these from least to greatest: −3, 0, −8, 2.
questions.explanation: The most negative number is smallest. Reading left to right on the line gives −8, −3, 0, 2.

questions.q: A submarine at −40 m rises 15 m. What is its new depth?
questions.explanation: Rising adds: −40 + 15. Different signs, so 40 − 15 = 25 with the larger sign (negative): −25 m.
Change to addition: −5 + (−6). Same signs, so add 5 + 6 = 11 and keep the negative sign: −11.

faq.a: Integers are the whole numbers, their negatives and zero — for example −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3. They do not include fractions or decimals. In Class 6 the focus is placing them on a number line and adding and subtracting them.

faq.q: Why is subtracting a negative the same as adding?
faq.a: Because taking away a debt leaves you better off. On the number line, subtracting means moving left, so subtracting a negative reverses that and moves right — the same direction as adding. That is why 8 − (−3) = 8 + 3 = 11.
−7 is smaller. The further left a number sits on the number line, the smaller it is, and −7 is further left than −3. It helps to think of temperature: −7°C is colder than −3°C.

faq.q: Can absolute value ever be negative?
faq.a: No. Absolute value is the distance of a number from zero, and distance is never negative. So both |−15| and |15| equal 15.
